claims.text: Atomic size mismatch produces local lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions are the primary mechanism governing hardness in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions are the primary mechanism governing strength in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
A relatively narrow atomic-size distribution results in lower local lattice distortion.
Replacing elements with chemically similar elements having more disparate atomic radii increases atomic-size mismatch.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch through such substitutions increases lattice distortion.
The proposed substitutions can increase atomic-size mismatch without significantly changing average electron concentration.
The proposed substitutions can increase atomic-size mismatch without significantly changing overall phase stability.
Increased local lattice distortion creates internal stress fields.
Distortion-induced internal stress fields act as barriers to dislocation nucleation.
Distortion-induced internal stress fields act as barriers to dislocation propagation.
Larger atomic-size differences increase resistance to dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion raises hardness.
The increased resistance to dislocation motion raises yield strength.
The modified alloy will have higher hardness than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The predicted mechanical-property improvement may be moderate because the mechanism is primarily active during dislocation-driven plasticity.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to single-phase HEAs at moderate temperatures and strain rates when deformation is governed primarily by dislocation motion.
The proposed relationship may fail when phase instability, diffusion-controlled mechanisms, or extreme-temperature effects dominate.
